finding.claim: The /settings/email POST endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing, account-modifying operation. It could allow changing or clearing an email for a null/unauthenticated user record, and it is inconsistent with /settings/password, which requires login. A CSRF-style or anonymous call is also possible, since no CSRF protection is present.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated HTTP client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, an account email change that is a precondition for account takeover via password reset

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None for anonymous callers, and does not abort
set_email(None, ...) is called without any auth check

finding.guards_checked: login_required exists (routes.py:8) but is not applied to this route. There is no in-handler check of g.uid. There is no CSRF protection or other middleware in the file. The /settings/password route correctly uses login_required (routes.py:42). set_email is a stub, so the real impact depends on its implementation, where a None uid could affect rows with NULL ids or raise an error.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_required at routes.py:8-16 exists but is not applied to this route; login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; no in-handler check of g.uid)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password, which uses login_required at routes.py:42. The impact is overstated because set_email is a stub (routes.py:48) and the email is hardcoded, so the missing authentication is real but the account-takeover claim is unproven.
